extracted.intended_audience: writers, dramatists, novelists, critics and readers interested in literary aesthetics and creative-writing principles
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and aesthetic criteria for producing and evaluating literature and the decorative arts that favour imaginative invention over literal realism; guidance about style, subject-matter, technique, and the social role of 'lying' in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying and poetry are arts requiring study
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Lying and poetry are arts ... and they require the most careful study, the most disinterested devotion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imaginative invention as a craft: learn technique, practise, and cultivate the imaginative faculty. Wilde compares the liar/poet to practitioners of painting and sculpture who have 'subtle secrets of form and colour'—practice must precede perfection. Anti-pattern: falling into ’careless habits of accuracy’ or becoming habitually truthful, which kills imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is a veil, not a mirror (do not judge art by resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Art is not to be judged by any external standard of resemblance. She is a veil, rather than a mirror.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value invention and internal coherence over literal resemblance to life. Art may create forms and beings 'more real than living man.' Anti-pattern: evaluating artistic success by factual accuracy or similarity to lived experience (realism-as-mirror).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative creation over factual reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The only real people are the people who never existed ... If a novelist is base enough to go to life for his personages he should at least pretend that they are creations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent characters and situations rather than copying or boasting about real-life sources. Boasting that characters are taken directly from life robs them of vitality. Anti-pattern: local colour and literal transcription of acquaintances or events; claiming autobiography for characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and limitation are the conditions of art
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In der Beschränkung zeigt Fsich erst der Meister ... the limitation, the very condition of any art is style.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work within formal limits and cultivate distinctive style, cadence and diction. Mastery appears through disciplined form and chosen constraints. Anti-pattern: formlessness or slavish transcription of life that abandons style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and exaggeration as legitimate artistic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Art itself is really a form of exaggeration; and selection, which is the very spirit of art, is nothing more than an intensified mode of over-emphasis.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selection and heightened emphasis to create beauty and meaning. Emphasise, magnify, and invent to achieve artistic effect rather than merely reporting facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naturalistic, documentary realism
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The popular cry of our time is “Let us return to Life and Nature” ... but Life is the solvent that breaks up Art.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism that attempts faithful reproduction of life tends to vulgarise and sterilise art. Examples of the anti-pattern include melodrama and naturalistic novels that focus on tedious factual detail. Prefer imaginative reshaping to documentary method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-readability as a test of literature
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If one cannot enjoy reading a book over and over again, there is no use reading it at all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a work rewards repeated reading as an index of its literary value. Works that lose appeal after the first reading may lack the depth, style, or imaginative power that define literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subject-matter that does not merely concern us
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The only beautiful things, as somebody once said, are the things that do not concern us.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer remote, mythic, decorative, or non-utilitarian subjects over immediate, useful, or topical content. Avoid making the merely useful or socially immediate the primary subject of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer masks and archetypes to exhaustive psychological analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘What is interesting about people in good society ... is the mask that each one of them wears, not the reality that lies behind the mask.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on roles, masks, archetypes and dramatic persona rather than interminable inward analysis. Anti-pattern: novels of minute psychological parsing (the roman psychologique) that exhaust interest by over-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow invention that violates natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘She can draw the moon from heaven with a scarlet thread ... bid the almond-tree blossom in winter, and send the snow upon the ripe cornfield.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant imaginative licence to depict miracles, impossibilities, and fantastical elements when they serve the work’s aesthetic purpose. Do not feel bound by realism’s physical constraints when invention enriches beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: The aim of (artful) lying is to charm and give pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘For the aim of the liar is simply to charm, to delight, to give pleasure. He is the very basis of civilised society.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise delight, charm and aesthetic pleasure over moral instruction, didacticism, or purely informative aims. Artistic falsehood is justified by its capacity to enchant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is a matter of style
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Truth is entirely and absolutely a matter of style.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that what appears as ‘truth’ in art is framed and produced by style—how something is said determines its apparent truth. Evaluate works by stylistic adequacy, not mere factual truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique, musicality and rhythmic utterance matter
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘As one knows the poet by his fine music, so one can recognise the liar by his rich rhythmic utterance.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to cadence, musicality, phrase-making and rhetorical craft. A well-shaped utterance signals imaginative authority. Training in these techniques is mandatory for the imaginative writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of modernity of form and subject as vulgarising
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Pure modernity of form is always somewhat vulgarising ... We have mistaken the common livery of the age for the vesture of the Muses.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about adopting contemporary modes or topical subjects simply because they are current; novelty for its own sake can degrade artistic quality. Seek enduring aesthetic values rather than fashionable immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid documentary or encyclopaedic methods in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Blue-Book is rapidly becoming his ideal both for method and manner ... He has his tedious document humain ... shamelessly reading up his subject.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let research and factual accumulation replace imagination. Overreliance on encyclopaedic detail produces lifeless fiction. Research should inform but not dominate the imaginative act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative arts should use convention and invention, not faithful copy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The proper school to learn art in is not Life but Art ... Wherever we have returned to Life and Nature, our work has always become vulgar, common and uninteresting.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In decorative arts (tapestry, glass, carpets), prefer artistic convention, pattern and invention over literal depiction of natural objects. Learn from non-imitative traditions (Orientalism/Byzantine) rather than from slavish natural representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reveal or boast about real-life prototypes
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Nobody can possibly care for Delobelle ... now that we have learned ... that these characters were taken directly from life. To us they seem to have suddenly lost all their vitality.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the fiction fictional: disclosing that characters were copied from real persons diminishes their artistic power. Present creations as creations, not as transcriptions of life.
